prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

If you're not sure about something, just say so.

response.content:
Based on the provided search results, here are the official statements from the Python Software Foundation and CPython developers regarding the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build.

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "The free-threaded build has additional overhead when executing Python code compared to the default GIL-enabled build." | CLAIM: Official Python documentation acknowledges that the free-threaded build incurs a performance overhead compared to the default GIL-enabled build.
SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: Official Python documentation quantifies the single-threaded execution overhead of the free-threaded build as ranging from 1% to 8% depending on the hardware.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for --disable-gil builds." | CLAIM: PEP 703 states that the internal changes required to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL inherently increase execution overhead.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "For thread-safety reasons, an application running with multiple threads will only specialize a given bytecode once; this is why the overhead for programs that use multiple threads is larger compared to programs that only use one thread." | CLAIM: PEP 703 explains that multi-threaded programs have larger execution overhead than single-threaded ones due to bytecode specialization restrictions.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The largest contribution to execution overhead is biased reference counting followed by per-object locking." | CLAIM: PEP 703 identifies biased reference counting and per-object locking as the primary factors contributing to the execution overhead.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "Note that this PEP would not affect the performance of the default (non --disable-gil) builds of CPython." | CLAIM: PEP 703 asserts that the performance impact is strictly isolated to the free-threaded build, and standard GIL-enabled builds will not be affected.
SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "At this point we’re expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%." | CLAIM: The Steering Council's acceptance of PEP 703 outlines an expected worst-case performance penalty of 10% to 15% for the free-threaded build.
SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "The performance impact should be isolated to a free-threaded build; a GIL build should not see any performance impact in existing code." | CLAIM: The Steering Council mandates that any performance impact must be confined to the free-threaded build, ensuring existing GIL builds suffer no regressions.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "The performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%)." | CLAIM: PEP 779 reports that current single-threaded performance penalties hover around 10% on Linux/Windows and 3% on macOS.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance)." | CLAIM: PEP 779 reports the memory use overhead of the free-threaded build to be approximately 15-20% higher than the with-GIL build.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "We propose a target of 20% (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance) for phase II." | CLAIM: PEP 779 proposes a hard target of a maximum 20% memory use overhead for the officially supported "Phase II" stage of free-threading.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "we propose 15% as a hard performance target." | CLAIM: PEP 779 proposes a hard performance target allowing for a maximum 15% slowdown for the officially supported "Phase II" stage of free-threading.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Realistically, though, higher memory use is the cost of having efficient, safe free-threading, and we are unlikely to get this very close to the with-GIL build’s memory use without significant performance cost." | CLAIM: PEP 779 acknowledges that higher memory usage is an unavoidable cost for safe and efficient free-threading, and that minimizing it would significantly hurt CPU performance.
